opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this was work led by Chris Lu, the Discovered Policy Optimisation paper. The setup was that we didn't want to meta-learn some giant black-box neural network that replaces the whole RL algorithm, because then you learn very little. Instead we took the mirror learning framework, which gives you a space of drift functions that all come with theoretical guarantees, and we meta-learned within that space. PPO's clipping is just one point in that space, so we could ask: if you let evolution search over these drift functions, what does it find?

The interesting thing was that what came out wasn't just "PPO with a slightly different epsilon." It had qualitatively different structure. First, it was asymmetric. It treated the cases where the advantage is positive and where it's negative differently, and it treated the probability ratio going up differently from it going down. PPO is basically symmetric in a way that's a design choice, not something principled, and the meta-learner happily broke that symmetry.

Second, it had something like a rollback effect. Rather than just going flat outside the trust region, which is what PPO's clipping does (the gradient becomes zero), the learned objective actively pushed the policy back when the ratio drifted too far in certain directions. People had proposed rollback-style variants of PPO by hand before, so it was nice to see the meta-learner rediscover something in that family on its own.

What I found most exciting is that the result was interpretable. Because we'd constrained the search to this low-dimensional, theoretically grounded space, we could plot the learned function, look at it, and say, "okay, I understand what it's doing." Then Chris distilled that into a closed-form objective that you can just write down and drop into a PPO codebase, and it transferred to environments it was never trained on.

For me that's the broader lesson. Meta-learning works best when you combine it with the right inductive biases. Don't throw away everything we know theoretically; use the theory to carve out a good search space, then let the data tell you which corner of that space you should actually be in. And sometimes the answer is something a human wouldn't have designed, even though it makes perfect sense in hindsight.

r001.rationale: The response describes asymmetric handling of positive and negative advantages and a rollback effect beyond the trust region, but it does not state that further movement is more readily permitted for small advantages than for large ones.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this was the Learned Policy Optimisation work, LPO, where we took the PPO setup and basically replaced the hand-designed surrogate objective with a small neural network, and then meta-evolved that network across a distribution of environments in JAX. The whole thing only became feasible because of the end-to-end vectorisation; you can run thousands of PPO training runs in parallel on a single accelerator, so the outer loop stops being prohibitively expensive.

The thing that surprised us about the clipping is that we didn't put it in, and it came out anyway. PPO's clipping is this very particular design decision: you take the ratio between the new and the old policy, and once it moves outside of one plus or minus epsilon you flatten the gradient to zero so the policy can't move any further on that sample. It's a hack, in the best sense. It's an approximation to a trust region. And when we looked at what the learned objective was doing as a function of that same ratio and the advantage, it had carved out something that looks very much like that. There's a region where it pushes the policy, and then it stops pushing. Nobody told it that a trust region was a good idea; it discovered that moving too far on a single batch of data is harmful and found a way to prevent it.

But what I found more interesting is where it didn't match PPO. PPO's clipping is asymmetric in a slightly weird way: it only clips on the side where the update would improve the objective, so for a positive advantage you clip the ratio from above and for a negative advantage from below. The learned objective was more nuanced about this. It had what we ended up calling rollback behaviour, where if the ratio had drifted too far, the gradient didn't just go to zero, it actually turned around and pulled the policy back towards the old one. So instead of a flat plateau outside the trust region, you get a gentle restoring force. And on the other side, where PPO lets the ratio drift as far as it wants because moving in that direction is "safe", the learned objective was also cautious. It treated large deviations as something to be suspicious of regardless of the sign of the advantage.

And when we then looked at this more carefully, we realised it was also doing something like an entropy regulariser implicitly. The shape of the loss near a ratio of one was slightly tilted in a way that discouraged the policy from collapsing too quickly, which is exactly the kind of thing people add by hand with an entropy bonus. So you've got three fairly standard pieces of PPO folklore, the trust region, some asymmetry handling, and entropy regularisation, all falling out of a few hours of evolution on a GPU.

What that told me is twofold. First, a lot of the intuitions we've accumulated as a community are actually right, which is reassuring, because the learned objective rediscovered them from scratch. But second, the hand-designed version is a sort of piecewise-linear caricature of what you actually want, and there's a smoother, better-behaved object sitting right next to it. And the really nice part was that we could then read off those features and write down a tiny analytical modification to PPO, discovered policy optimisation, that captures most of the gain without needing the network at all. So the meta-learning became a tool for scientific discovery rather than a black box you have to deploy.

r001.rationale: The response says the learned objective is cautious about large deviations regardless of advantage sign, but does not state that it permits more movement for small advantages than for large ones.

astra-6.text: What I found interesting was that it rediscovered something like clipping, but it wasn’t simply reproducing PPO. In PPO, you clip based on how far the probability ratio has moved away from one. The learned objective also depended on the advantage, so those two quantities interacted in deciding when to stop pushing an update. That’s a useful distinction: you might want a different amount of movement depending on how good or bad the action appears to be. So it recovered this familiar idea of limiting updates, but with a more flexible rule than the one we typically write down by hand.

r001.rationale: The response says advantage and probability ratio interact in deciding when to stop an update, but does not state that beyond the clipping region further movement is permitted more readily for small advantages than for large ones.

sol-6.1.text:
What I found interesting was that we hadn’t explicitly built clipping into it, but the meta-learned objective developed something that looked very much like clipping. So there was a qualitative resemblance to PPO, even though it wasn’t simply reproducing PPO’s fixed clipping rule.

That’s quite interesting because clipping is a design choice we normally make by hand. Here, the outer optimization could discover that limiting the influence of certain updates was useful for learning. And the differences from the hand-designed objective are potentially the most informative part: they give us something to investigate, rather than just another set of hyperparameters.

r001.rationale: The response describes a clipping-like effect but does not state that beyond the clipping region, small advantages permit more movement from the reference policy than large advantages.
